description_full: Veralto Corporation provides water analytics, water treatment, marking and coding, and packaging and color solutions worldwide. It operates through two segments, Water Quality (WQ) and Product Quality & Innovation (PQI). The WQ segment offers precision instrumentation and water treatment technologies to measure, analyze, and treat water in residential, commercial, municipal, industrial, research, and natural resource applications under the Hach, Trojan Technologies, ChemTreat, and other brands. This segment also provides water solutions, including chemical reagents, services, and software solutions. The PQI segment offers marking and coding for packaged goods and related consumables; a software solution that provides digital asset management, marketing resource management, and product information management; inline printing solutions for products and packaging with marking and coding systems; design software and imaging systems for the creation of new packaging designs; color management solutions for printed packages and consumer and industrial products; and color standard services for the design industry. This segment sells its products and services through the Videojet, Linx, Esko, X-Rite, and Pantone brands. The company serves industries, such as municipal utilities, food and beverage, pharmaceutical, and industrials. The company was formerly known as DH EAS Holding Corp. and changed its name to Veralto Corporation in February 2023. Veralto Corporation was incorporated in 2022 and is headquartered in Waltham, Massachusetts.

financial_summary: Veralto Corp is a large-cap industrials business with a $28.8B market cap on $5.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 27% against a 8% cost of capital — a 19-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 60% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.0B in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.15× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 13× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.4%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.1× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.

The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 6%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $82.32 to $132 (P10-P90).

prof: ROIC of 27% clears the cost of capital of 7.8% by 19pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.02).
It runs a 60% gross margin and converts 18% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.15x.
ROE of 30% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 4.8% of revenue on R&D and 1.3% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.5x net debt to EBITDA ($2.0B of cash against $2.7B of debt), with interest covered 13.3x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.6, in the safe zone).
Goodwill makes up 37% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.7% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 21% of profits supports about 5.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.01, a backlog worth 6% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 13%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.8x, 1.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 7.8% on average.
Analysts expect 7.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (17 sales, net $8.0M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.4% (0.4% in dividends).
people: With about 17,000 employees, each generates about $324K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 4.7% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $60K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.3M (13x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
